question_text: Define the core economic problem of 'scarcity'.

key_points.text: We have unlimited wants and needs
The resources (like time, money, and materials) we have are limited
Because of this, we cannot have everything we want
Scarcity forces us to make difficult choices every day

question_text: What is 'opportunity cost'?

key_points.text: It is the value of the thing you chose not to do
It is the 'next best' choice that you gave up
When you buy a pizza, the opportunity cost might be the burger you didn't buy
Opportunity cost helps you decide the true cost of a decision

question_text: Give an example of a resource that is scarce.

key_points.text: Time: You only have 24 hours in a day for school, sleep, and fun
Money: You have a limited amount in your wallet or bank account
Land: There is only a fixed amount of space to build houses or farms
Oil/Gas: These natural resources can run out or are expensive to get

question_text: Explain the difference between a need and a want.

key_points.text: A 'need' is something you must have to survive (like food, water, and shelter)
A 'want' is something nice to have but you can live without (like a new game console)
Needs are often the same for everyone, but wants change a lot
Economics looks at how we use scarce resources to satisfy our needs and wants

question_text: How does scarcity force the government to make choices?

key_points.text: The money the government collects (from taxes) is limited
They must decide where to spend this money (a big choice)
For example, choosing between building new schools or improving hospitals
Every choice has an opportunity cost, which is the other important thing they didn't fund

question_text: What is the primary function of exchange in an economy?

key_points.text: It allows people to trade what they have for what they want or need
It makes sure resources end up where they are most needed (optimal allocation)
It lets people and countries focus on what they are best at (specialization)
Exchange increases the total amount of goods and services available to everyone

question_text: Explain 'division of labor'.

key_points.text: It means breaking up a large job (like building a car) into many smaller tasks
Each worker focuses on only one of these smaller, specific tasks
Workers become very fast and skilled at their single task (specialization)
This makes production much quicker and more efficient (more things made with less time)

question_text: What is 'barter' and what is its main drawback?

key_points.text: Barter is trading goods or services directly for other goods or services
You swap your apples for someone's bread without using money
Drawback: It requires a 'double coincidence of wants'
This means you must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have (very difficult!)

question_text: List four functions of money.

key_points.text: Medium of Exchange: It is generally accepted by everyone for buying and selling
Unit of Account: It is a way to measure and compare the value of different things (e.g., this car is €20,000)
Store of Value: You can save it now to spend it later (it holds its value)
Standard of Deferred Payment: It is used to settle debts that will be paid in the future

question_text: What is the concept of 'comparative advantage'?

key_points.text: It means a person or country can produce something at a lower opportunity cost
Even if another country is better at producing everything (absolute advantage)
It's the main reason why countries specialize and trade with each other
Trading based on comparative advantage makes both sides richer

question_text: How does money make the exchange process smoother?

key_points.text: Money solves the 'double coincidence of wants' problem of barter
You don't need to find a direct swapper, you just sell for money and buy with money
It makes it faster and easier to know the value of what you are trading
It reduces the time and effort people spend on trading (transaction costs)

question_text: Define the term 'market' in economics.

key_points.text: A market is not always a physical place (like a store or street market)
It is any place or way (like online) where buyers and sellers meet to trade
The interaction between buyers and sellers decides the price and quantity
Examples: the market for mobile phones, the labor market, the housing market

question_text: What is the role of price in coordinating choices in a market?

key_points.text: Price acts as a signal to consumers and producers
High price signals producers to make more of a good (because it's profitable)
High price signals consumers to buy less of a good (because it's expensive)
Price changes help bring the amount supplied and the amount demanded into balance

question_text: Define 'demand'.

key_points.text: Demand is the amount of a product or service
That consumers are willing and financially able to buy
At a certain price, during a certain period of time
The demand curve usually slopes downwards: people buy less when the price is high

question_text: State the Law of Demand.

key_points.text: The Law of Demand says that price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
When the price of a good goes up, people buy less of it
When the price of a good goes down, people buy more of it
This is true if all other things (like income and tastes) stay the same (ceteris paribus)

question_text: Define 'supply'.

key_points.text: Supply is the amount of a product or service
That producers (companies) are willing and able to offer for sale
At a certain price, during a certain period of time
The supply curve usually slopes upwards: producers offer more when the price is high

question_text: State the Law of Supply.

key_points.text: The Law of Supply says that price and quantity supplied move in the same direction
When the price of a good goes up, producers want to sell more of it (for more profit)
When the price of a good goes down, producers want to sell less of it
This is true if all other factors (like costs of production) stay the same (ceteris paribus)

question_text: What is 'market equilibrium'?

key_points.text: It is the balanced point in the market
It happens when the quantity demanded by buyers is exactly equal to the quantity supplied by sellers
The price at this point is the 'equilibrium price' or 'market price'
At this point, the market is 'cleared', and there is no shortage or surplus

question_text: Explain what a 'surplus' is and how the market corrects it.

key_points.text: A surplus (or excess supply) happens when the price is too high
Producers supply more goods than consumers want to buy
The market corrects it: Sellers lower the price to get rid of the extra stock
As the price drops, demand goes up and supply goes down until equilibrium is reached

question_text: Explain what a 'shortage' is and how the market corrects it.

key_points.text: A shortage (or excess demand) happens when the price is too low
Consumers want to buy more goods than producers are supplying
The market corrects it: Buyers compete with each other and are willing to pay more
As the price goes up, demand goes down and supply goes up until equilibrium is reached

question_text: What are the four main market structures (market forms)?

key_points.text: Perfect Competition: Many small sellers, identical products (e.g., agricultural products)
Monopolistic Competition: Many sellers, slightly different products (e.g., restaurants, clothing stores)
Oligopoly: A few large sellers dominate the market (e.g., mobile phone providers)
Monopoly: Only one seller in the entire market (e.g., a local water company)

question_text: What is the key characteristic of a 'monopoly'?

key_points.text: There is only one single company that sells the product or service
The product has no close substitutes (no real alternatives)
The company has complete control over setting the price (they are a 'price maker')
It is almost impossible for new companies to start selling in that market (high barriers to entry)

question_text: What is 'intertemporal exchange'?

key_points.text: It is an economic exchange that involves time
It means you are trading something now for something in the future
The most common examples are saving and borrowing (taking out a loan)
Saving means giving up money/spending now to get more money/spending later

question_text: What is the price that coordinates intertemporal exchange?

key_points.text: The 'interest rate'
Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow money
Interest is the extra money you earn when you save money
It is the price paid for the use of money over time

question_text: Explain the role of interest for households (families).

key_points.text: When they save money in a bank, the bank pays them interest (an income)
When they borrow money (like a mortgage for a house), they must pay interest (a cost)
High interest makes borrowing expensive and saving attractive
Low interest makes borrowing cheap and saving less attractive

question_text: Explain the role of interest for businesses (firms).

key_points.text: If a business needs a loan to buy a new machine, interest is the cost of that loan
The interest rate affects whether a new investment (like a new factory) is profitable
Lower interest rates encourage businesses to borrow money and invest more
If interest rates rise, businesses may cancel or postpone their investment plans

question_text: How does 'inflation' affect the real value of savings over time?

key_points.text: Inflation is when prices of goods and services go up generally
Inflation causes the purchasing power of your money to go down
If the bank's interest rate is lower than the inflation rate, your savings can buy less later on
So, inflation 'eats away' at the real value (what you can buy) of your saved money

question_text: What is the concept of 'risk' in intertemporal exchange?

key_points.text: Risk is the chance that the future will not turn out as expected
For banks, the main risk is that a borrower will not pay back the loan (default risk)
The riskier the loan (e.g., lending to a new, small company), the higher the interest rate will be
Investors also face the risk that the value of their savings/investments will fall

question_text: Give an example of 'exchange over time' for the government.

key_points.text: When the government needs to pay for a big project now (like a new highway)
It often borrows money by selling 'government bonds' to investors (people and businesses)
This is a promise to pay the money back later, plus interest
This borrowing is an exchange: money now for a larger amount of money later

question_text: Why do individuals often prefer consumption now over consumption later?

key_points.text: They have a 'time preference' or are simply impatient to enjoy things
They face uncertainty about the future (e.g., they might be ill or not alive later)
Money now can be invested and earn interest, making it worth more than the same amount later
This preference is why people need to be paid interest to save or delay spending

question_text: Explain why cooperation can be more beneficial than individual action when interests conflict.

key_points.text: If everyone acts selfishly, the result is often worse for everyone (like the 'Prisoner's Dilemma')
Cooperation (like negotiating a deal) can lead to a 'win-win' result
It helps avoid negative outcomes like price wars between companies
Working together allows parties to share costs and benefits, achieving a bigger total gain

question_text: What is a 'collective good' (or public good)?

key_points.text: A good that is 'non-excludable' (you cannot stop people who haven't paid from using it)
A good that is 'non-rivalrous' (one person using it does not stop others from using it)
Examples are national defence, public street lighting, or clean air
These goods are usually provided by the government and paid for with taxes

question_text: What is the 'free-rider problem'?

key_points.text: It happens with collective goods because they are non-excludable
Individuals can benefit from the good or service without paying for it (they 'free-ride')
If everyone free-rides, no one will pay, and the good will not be produced
This problem often leads to the government having to force people to pay (via taxes) to provide the good

question_text: How can 'coercion' (centralization) resolve the free-rider problem?

key_points.text: Coercion means the government uses force or rules to make people act a certain way
The government enforces payment through mandatory taxes for public services
This forces everyone to contribute, stopping people from free-riding
It can also be used to enforce rules, like mandatory vaccination or environmental regulations

question_text: Give an example of cooperation between businesses.

key_points.text: A 'Joint Venture': Two or more companies work together on a specific project or product
Lobbying: Companies in the same industry cooperate to influence new government laws
Creating Industry Standards: They agree on common sizes or quality rules for products
Forming a Cartel (often illegal): Secretly agreeing to fix prices or limit supply to maximize profit

question_text: What is the purpose of a 'collective labor agreement' (CAO in Dutch)?

key_points.text: It is a contract that covers all the workers in a whole sector or company (not just one person)
It is the result of negotiation and cooperation between trade unions (workers) and employers' organizations
It sets the rules for working conditions, like wages, holidays, and working hours
It ensures that all workers in that group have at least the same minimum terms of employment

question_text: What is an 'externality'?

key_points.text: An externality is a side effect of an economic activity (production or consumption)
This side effect affects a third party (someone who is not the buyer or seller)
The cost or benefit is not included in the market price of the good or service
Examples: pollution (negative) or a well-maintained garden next door (positive)

question_text: Give an example of a negative externality.

key_points.text: Factory Pollution: A factory dumps waste into a river, damaging the environment for local people
Traffic Jam: People driving their cars cause noise, air pollution, and time loss for others
Loud Music: Someone playing very loud music late at night disturbs their neighbors' sleep
Overfishing: One company overfishing damages the fish stock for everyone else

question_text: How can government intervention (centralization) address a negative externality?

key_points.text: Taxes: The government can put a 'Pigouvian tax' on the activity (e.g., a tax on carbon emissions)
Regulations: The government can set strict rules or limits (e.g., how much pollution a factory can produce)
Bans: In extreme cases, they can ban the harmful product or activity completely
Subsidies: They can give money to encourage people to use cleaner alternatives instead (e.g., electric cars)

question_text: What is a 'budget line' (or budget constraint) for a household?

key_points.text: It is a line on a graph that shows all the possible combinations of two goods you can buy
It is based on the total amount of money (income) you have to spend
The slope of the line shows the trade-off (opportunity cost) between the two goods
Any point outside the line is too expensive, and any point inside the line means you haven't spent all your money

question_text: How does an increase in income affect a consumer's budget line?

key_points.text: If your income goes up, you have more money to spend in total
The budget line will shift outwards, away from the origin
This means you can afford to buy more of both goods than before
The slope of the line (the relative prices) will usually stay the same, as prices haven't changed

question_text: What is the purpose of 'financial key figures' (financial ratios) for a business?

key_points.text: They are simple calculations (like a percentage) used to understand a company's financial health
They help check if a company is profitable (making money)
They help check if a company is liquid (can pay its short-term bills)
They are used by investors and banks to decide whether to lend money or buy shares in the company

question_text: What is a 'subsidy' and how does it affect the market?

key_points.text: A subsidy is a sum of money given by the government to a producer or consumer
The goal is usually to encourage the production or consumption of a certain good
It lowers the cost of production for the supplier (the supply curve shifts right)
The result is a lower market price for the consumer and a larger quantity of the good being sold

question_text: Define 'price elasticity of demand' ($E_d$).

key_points.text: It measures how much the quantity demanded changes
When the price of the good changes (how sensitive buyers are to price changes)
If a small price change leads to a large quantity change, demand is 'elastic'
If a large price change leads to only a small quantity change, demand is 'inelastic'

question_text: If a small price increase on a necessary medicine causes very few people to stop buying it, is the demand elastic or inelastic?

key_points.text: The demand is 'inelastic'
This means the change in quantity demanded is proportionally less than the price change
Medicine is often inelastic because it is a necessity (people need it regardless of price)
For inelastic goods, a price increase will increase the total revenue for the seller

question_text: If a firm operates in a perfectly competitive market, what is its relationship with the market price?

key_points.text: The firm is a 'price taker'
They must accept the price set by the forces of total market supply and demand
If they charge a slightly higher price, customers will buy from another seller (since products are identical)
They have no individual control over the market price

question_text: What is 'disposable income' for a household?

key_points.text: It is the money a household has left after all taxes and social contributions are paid
It is the actual amount of money that is available to spend or save
It is an important factor that determines how much a household can consume
Disposable Income = Gross Income - Taxes - Social Contributions

question_text: How does a decrease in the interest rate generally affect borrowing and saving behavior?

key_points.text: Borrowing: It becomes cheaper to take out loans (e.g., mortgages or personal loans)
This encourages households and businesses to borrow and spend/invest more
Saving: The return (interest earned) on savings in the bank becomes lower
This makes people less motivated to save their money

question_text: What is a 'collective action problem'?

key_points.text: A situation where all individuals would be better off if they all cooperated
But each individual has a strong incentive to 'cheat' or act only in their own interest
The result of everyone acting selfishly is a worse outcome for the entire group
This is why rules or central authority (like government) are sometimes needed to force cooperation

question_text: Give an example of a policy choice involving a trade-off due to scarcity (Domain B).

key_points.text: Choice: The government has a limited budget for public services
Action: Deciding to spend more money on better education for students
Trade-off: This means less money is available to spend on improving roads or healthcare
Scarcity of money forces the choice: more of one thing means less of another

question_text: What is the main goal of a profit-maximizing firm?

key_points.text: To make its total profit as large as possible
Profit is the difference between the money they earn (Total Revenue) and the money they spend (Total Cost)
They achieve this by producing the quantity where the extra money earned from the last product equals the extra cost of making it ($MR = MC$)
This goal guides all their major decisions, like what to produce and how much to charge

question_text: What are 'fixed costs' for a business?

key_points.text: Costs that do not change, no matter how much the company produces or sells (in the short run)
They must be paid even if the company produces nothing
Examples include the monthly rent for a building or the salary of a permanent manager
Fixed Costs + Variable Costs = Total Costs

question_text: What are 'variable costs' for a business?

key_points.text: Costs that change directly with the amount of goods or services produced (the output)
If production increases, these costs go up; if production stops, these costs disappear
Examples include the cost of raw materials, hourly wages for production workers, and electricity used by machines
They are zero when the production level is zero

question_text: How is 'productivity' measured in economics?

key_points.text: It is a measure of how efficiently goods and services are produced
It is calculated by taking the total output (what is made)
And dividing it by the amount of input used (like labor or capital)
Example: Output per hour worked (Labor Productivity)

question_text: Why is 'specialization' important for a country's welfare?

key_points.text: Specialization means a country focuses on producing the goods it is best at (comparative advantage)
This leads to increased efficiency and lower production costs for those goods
By trading these goods with other countries, the country can consume a greater variety of goods
Overall, it increases the total wealth and standard of living for the country's people

question_text: What is a 'price floor' and what is its potential consequence?

key_points.text: A price floor is a minimum price set by the government that is above the equilibrium price
The price cannot legally fall below this level (e.g., minimum wage)
Consequence: It leads to a 'surplus' (excess supply)
More is supplied at the high price than is demanded (e.g., unemployment in the labor market)

question_text: What is a 'price ceiling' and what is its potential consequence?

key_points.text: A price ceiling is a maximum price set by the government that is below the equilibrium price
The price cannot legally rise above this level (e.g., maximum rent control)
Consequence: It leads to a 'shortage' (excess demand)
More is demanded at the low price than is supplied (e.g., long waiting lists or black markets)

question_text: What is 'price discrimination'?

key_points.text: It is when a seller charges different prices for the exact same good or service
The different prices are charged to different groups of customers
Examples: Student discounts, senior citizen discounts, or different ticket prices based on when you buy a flight
The seller does this to capture more consumer surplus and maximize profit

question_text: In the context of the business cycle, what is a 'recession'?

key_points.text: A recession is a period when the economy is shrinking or declining
It is officially defined as a fall in the Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for two quarters (six months) in a row
During a recession, companies make less, people lose jobs (unemployment rises), and confidence is low
It is the opposite of an 'economic boom' or expansion

question_text: Define 'Gross Domestic Product (GDP)'.

key_points.text: GDP is the total money value of all the final goods and services
That are produced within a country's borders
Over a specific period of time (usually one year)
It is the most common way to measure the size and health of a country's economy

question_text: What is the difference between 'nominal GDP' and 'real GDP'?

key_points.text: Nominal GDP: Measured using the current prices of that year (it can be inflated by rising prices)
Real GDP: Measured using the prices from a fixed 'base year' (it is adjusted for inflation)
Real GDP is the better measure for actual economic growth
Because it only shows if the quantity of goods and services has truly increased

question_text: What is 'monetary policy' and who is typically responsible for it in the Eurozone?

key_points.text: Monetary policy is what the central bank does to control the money supply and interest rates
Its main goal is to control inflation and support economic growth
In the Netherlands and other Eurozone countries, the European Central Bank (ECB) is responsible
The ECB's main tool is setting the official interest rate for banks

question_text: What is 'fiscal policy' and who is typically responsible for it in the Netherlands?

key_points.text: Fiscal policy is the government's plan to use spending and taxation to influence the economy
The government decides how much to spend (e.g., on infrastructure) and how much tax to collect
The national government (Ministers and Parliament) is responsible for it
During a recession, they might increase spending (stimulus) or cut taxes to boost the economy

question_text: What is the main goal of the European Central Bank (ECB)?

key_points.text: The primary goal is to maintain 'price stability' in the Eurozone (countries using the Euro)
This means keeping inflation low and predictable
Their official target is to keep inflation at 2% over the medium term
A stable price level is important for consumers and businesses to plan for the future

question_text: What is the primary indicator of inflation used in the Eurozone?

key_points.text: The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)
This index tracks the price changes of a 'basket' of goods and services that a typical household buys
It is 'harmonised' so that all countries in the Eurozone measure inflation in the same way
It is the main number the ECB uses to see if they are meeting their inflation target

question_text: How does a government budget deficit relate to 'exchange over time' (Domain E)?

key_points.text: A budget deficit means the government's spending is more than its income (taxes) in a year
To cover the deficit, the government must borrow money (often by issuing bonds)
This borrowing is an exchange over time: they get money now and promise to pay it back later with interest
The accumulated deficits over time become the 'national debt'

question_text: What is a 'stock' in economics, and give an example.

key_points.text: A 'stock' is a quantity that is measured at a specific point in time (like taking a snapshot)
It does not have a time dimension (it's not 'per day' or 'per year')
Example: A person's 'wealth' at the end of the year (what they own)
Other examples: The national debt, the capital of a company, or the total money supply

question_text: What is a 'flow' in economics, and give an example.

key_points.text: A 'flow' is a quantity that is measured over a period of time (like a video recording)
It always has a time dimension (e.g., 'per month' or 'per year')
Example: A person's 'income' per month (money flowing in)
Other examples: GDP, consumption, investment, government deficit/surplus

question_text: What is the significance of the 'price mechanism' in a market economy?

key_points.text: It is the way the market solves the three basic economic questions: what, how, and for whom to produce
Prices automatically adjust to coordinate the choices of millions of buyers and sellers
It acts as an invisible hand that allocates scarce resources efficiently
It ensures that goods are produced that people want and bought by those who can afford them

question_text: In a market, what is meant by 'homogeneity' of a product?

key_points.text: It means all the products offered by different sellers are identical or exactly the same
The buyer cannot tell the difference between one seller's product and another's
The only thing a buyer cares about is the price (they will always choose the cheapest)
It is a key feature of 'perfect competition' (e.g., a bag of rice or a barrel of crude oil)

question_text: What is 'asymmetric information'?

key_points.text: It means one party in an economic transaction knows more than the other party
The information is not 'symmetric' (equal) between buyer and seller
Example: The seller of a used car knows more about the car's hidden defects than the buyer
This can cause 'market failure' because the party with less information makes a bad choice

question_text: Give an example of a situation where negotiation is a better choice than individual action for a consumer.

key_points.text: Buying a large item like a house or a new car
By negotiating, the consumer can try to get a lower price than the initial offer
It can also lead to better terms, such as a longer warranty or included extra features
Individual action (just paying the sticker price) might cost the consumer much more money

question_text: What is the concept of 'rent-seeking'?

key_points.text: It means using resources (like time or money for lobbying) to try and gain extra wealth ('rent')
The goal is to get this wealth from others without actually creating new goods or services
Example: A company paying politicians to pass a law that unfairly benefits only them
This activity is seen as wasteful because it shifts wealth around instead of growing the total economy

question_text: Explain the concept of 'net wealth' for a household.

key_points.text: It is the total value of everything the household owns (their 'assets')
Minus the total value of everything the household owes (their 'liabilities' or debts)
Assets include house value, bank savings, and investments
Liabilities include mortgages, student loans, and credit card debt

question_text: What is the 'real interest rate'?

key_points.text: It is the interest rate you see at the bank (the 'nominal interest rate')
Minus the rate of inflation
It represents the true return on your savings or the true cost of your borrowing in terms of purchasing power
If nominal interest is 2% and inflation is 3%, the real interest rate is -1% (you are actually losing buying power)

question_text: What is the 'time value of money'?

key_points.text: It is the idea that money available now is worth more than the same amount of money in the future
This is because money now can be invested or saved to earn interest
Also, inflation will likely reduce the purchasing power of the future money
This concept is fundamental to all borrowing and saving decisions (Domain E)

question_text: Explain 'marginal cost'.

key_points.text: It is the extra cost a company has to pay
To produce one additional unit of a good or service
Example: The cost of the ingredients and the worker's time for one extra pizza
Firms use it to decide if making one more item is worth it

question_text: Explain 'marginal revenue'.

key_points.text: It is the extra money (revenue) a company earns
From selling one additional unit of a good or service
Example: The selling price of the one extra pizza the company sells
Firms use it to compare against marginal cost to decide how much to produce

question_text: What is the profit-maximising rule for a firm in any market structure?

key_points.text: The firm should produce the quantity of output
Where its Marginal Revenue ($MR$) is exactly equal to its Marginal Cost ($MC$)
If $MR > MC$, the firm should produce more (they make more extra profit)
If $MR < MC$, the firm should produce less (the last item cost more than it earned)

question_text: What is the difference between 'capital' and 'labor' as factors of production?

key_points.text: Labor is the human effort (physical and mental) used in production (workers)
Capital is the man-made resources used to produce other goods (machines, tools, buildings)
Labor is rewarded with wages and salaries
Capital is rewarded with interest or dividends

question_text: What is the effect on the market for a normal good if consumers' income increases?

key_points.text: A 'normal good' is one that people buy more of when their income goes up
The demand curve for that good will shift to the right (Demand increases)
This new, higher demand will cause the equilibrium price to rise
And the equilibrium quantity sold in the market will also increase

question_text: What is an 'inferior good'?

key_points.text: An inferior good is one that people buy less of
When their income goes up (they switch to a better/nicer alternative)
Example: Cheap public transport may be used less when people can afford a car
Example: Cheaper store-brand foods are bought less when people can afford premium brands

question_text: What is the primary way banks create new money (money creation)?

key_points.text: Banks create 'fiduciary money' (or 'deposit money') when they extend loans
When a bank approves a loan, they do not give physical cash, they just put a number in the borrower's bank account
This deposit is new money because it can now be spent by the borrower
This process is limited by the amount of cash the bank has and the rules of the Central Bank

question_text: Why is 'perfect information' a necessary condition for a perfectly competitive market?

key_points.text: It means all buyers and sellers know everything about the product, prices, and costs
If buyers know everything, no seller can charge a higher price than another (they must sell at the market price)
If producers know everything, they can make the best decisions on how to produce efficiently
Perfect information ensures that resources are allocated as efficiently as possible

question_text: What is the 'Prisoner's Dilemma' and which Domain does it illustrate?

key_points.text: It's a classic example in game theory showing a situation where two rational people choose not to cooperate
Each person chooses the option that is best for themselves individually
But the result of both acting selfishly is a worse outcome for both of them together
It illustrates Domain F (Cooperation and Negotiation) and the challenge of getting people to cooperate for a better collective result

question_text: How can a firm use 'product differentiation'?

key_points.text: It means making a product slightly different or unique from those of competitors
Firms use things like branding, quality differences, or better service to make their product stand out
Differentiation makes their product slightly less of a substitute for others
This gives the firm some 'market power' so they can raise their price a little without losing all their customers

question_text: What is 'consumption' in macroeconomic terms?

key_points.text: It is the total spending by households on final goods and services in the economy
It includes things like buying food, clothes, paying for holidays, and energy bills
It is a major part of the country's GDP (economic output)
It is a 'flow' variable, measured over a period of time

question_text: What is 'investment' in macroeconomic terms?

key_points.text: It is the spending by businesses (and sometimes government) on new capital goods
Capital goods are things like new machinery, equipment, factories, and buildings
The goal of investment is to increase the economy's ability to produce goods and services in the future
It is the part of GDP that drives long-term economic growth

question_text: Explain the concept of 'economic growth'.

key_points.text: It is an increase in a country's ability to produce goods and services over time
It is usually measured as a positive change in the Real GDP from one year to the next
Growth leads to more jobs, higher incomes, and a higher standard of living
It is often caused by new technology, more capital goods, or a larger, better-educated workforce

question_text: What is 'unemployment' and how is the unemployment rate calculated?

key_points.text: Unemployment refers to people who are able and willing to work
But they currently do not have a job and are actively looking for one
The Unemployment Rate is calculated as: (Number of Unemployed / Total Labor Force) x 100%
The Labor Force includes all people working or actively looking for work

question_text: What is 'debt-to-GDP ratio' and why is it important for a government?

key_points.text: It is the total amount of national debt (stock) divided by the country's GDP (flow)
It shows the total debt compared to the total size of the economy in a year
A high ratio suggests the country may struggle to pay back its debt or the interest on it
It is an important measure of a country's financial health and ability to borrow in the future

question_text: How does technology increase efficiency (Domain C)?

key_points.text: New technology (like robots or computers) can help workers produce much more in the same time
It reduces the amount of raw material or energy needed to make a product
This lowers the cost of production for companies
Higher efficiency leads to higher productivity, which makes the whole economy wealthier

question_text: What is the role of a 'financial intermediary' (e.g., a bank) in intertemporal exchange (Domain E)?

key_points.text: They connect people who have extra money (savers/lenders) with those who need money (borrowers)
They pool together small savings from many people into large loans
They manage the risk of lending by checking borrowers' credit and diversifying loans
They make the exchange over time possible and efficient (getting money from present to future uses)

question_text: Explain 'market failure'.

key_points.text: Market failure is a situation where the free market, by itself, fails to allocate resources efficiently
This means the market does not reach the best possible outcome for society
Causes include externalities (like pollution), public goods, or monopolies
Market failures are often reasons for government intervention and policy

question_text: What is a 'coordination mechanism' other than the market price?

key_points.text: Centralization or Planning: Decisions are made by a central authority (e.g., the government)
Coercion: Using rules, laws, or force to make people act in a certain way
Negotiation/Cooperation: Parties openly talk to reach an agreement that benefits both
Example: Traffic laws coordinate driving choices without needing a price

question_text: What is the key difference between a 'price maker' and a 'price taker'?

key_points.text: Price Taker: Must accept the market price (e.g., companies in perfect competition)
Price Maker: Has enough market power to set its own price (e.g., a monopoly or an oligopoly)
Price makers usually face a downward-sloping demand curve
Price takers face a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve

question_text: How does competition affect a company's profit and product price?

key_points.text: High competition forces companies to keep their product prices low
It also forces companies to be efficient and find ways to lower their production costs
Competition generally leads to lower profits for the companies
But it benefits consumers by giving them more choice and lower prices (increasing prosperity)

question_text: Explain the relationship between saving and investment in the economy.

key_points.text: Saving (money not spent on consumption) is the source of funds for investment
People save money by putting it in banks or buying bonds
Banks use these savings to give loans to businesses for investment projects (e.g., new machinery)
Therefore, increased saving can lead to increased investment and future economic growth

question_text: Why is the Dutch government interested in promoting comparative advantage?

key_points.text: It wants Dutch companies to specialize in products they can produce with the lowest opportunity cost
This allows the Netherlands to export those goods efficiently to other countries
These exports bring in money and wealth to the country (creating trade surplus)
Specialization and trade increase the overall national income and economic welfare

question_text: Explain one type of 'economic policy' (e.g., competition policy) and its goal (Domain D).

key_points.text: Policy: Competition Policy (enforced by the Authority for Consumers and Markets - ACM)
Goal: To prevent monopolies and cartels, and ensure markets remain competitive
Why: Competition keeps prices low for consumers and encourages innovation by firms
Result: This protection of the market leads to greater economic prosperity for consumers

question_text: Explain inflation

key_points.text: General increase in prices
Reduction of purchasing power

question_text: What are the three main factors of production (input resources)?

key_points.text: Labor: The human effort used in production
Capital: Man-made resources used to produce goods (like machinery and tools)
Natural Resources (Land): All raw materials from nature (like oil, water, and soil)
Entrepreneurship (sometimes added): The skill to combine the other three factors and take risks

question_text: How can a country increase its potential for economic growth?

key_points.text: Invest in better education and training (improving labor quality)
Spend money on research and development (creating new technologies)
Invest in new infrastructure (better roads, faster internet)
Encourage more investment in new factories and machinery (increasing capital)

question_text: Explain the concept of 'economic sectors' (primary, secondary, and tertiary).

key_points.text: Primary Sector: Extracting raw materials (e.g., farming, fishing, mining)
Secondary Sector: Manufacturing and processing raw materials into finished goods (e.g., factories, construction)
Tertiary Sector: Providing services (e.g., banks, schools, hospitals, retail stores)
In rich countries like the Netherlands, most people work in the Tertiary Sector (services)

question_text: What is the relationship between 'wealth' and 'income'?

key_points.text: Income is a flow; the money a person or household earns over a period of time (like salary or wages)
Wealth is a stock; the total value of assets owned at a specific point in time (like savings or property)
A high income allows a person to increase their wealth quickly through saving and investment
Wealth can generate income (e.g., rental income from property or interest from savings)

question_text: How does competition lead to innovation?

key_points.text: To survive, companies must try to be better than their rivals (competition)
This forces them to invent new products or find cheaper, better ways to produce them (innovation)
Innovation can give a company a temporary advantage, allowing them to earn a higher profit
In the long run, this benefits all consumers with better, cheaper products

question_text: What is the key characteristic that distinguishes an 'oligopoly' market structure?

key_points.text: The market is dominated by a small number of large firms (e.g., mobile phone networks, large soft drink companies)
The products can be similar or differentiated (e.g., different car brands)
Each firm's actions (like changing price) strongly affect the others
They often face the choice between competing aggressively or cooperating to keep prices high (Domain F)

question_text: Explain why saving money is an example of exchange over time.

key_points.text: When you save, you give up spending (consumption) now (the present)
In exchange, you gain the ability to spend a larger amount of money later (the future)
The interest earned is the 'price' you receive for delaying your spending
The exchange is between present consumption and future consumption

question_text: What is a 'business cycle'?

key_points.text: It is the up and down movement of a country's economic activity (GDP) over time
It consists of four main phases: boom (peak), recession (contraction), trough, and recovery (expansion)
These cycles are irregular; they do not happen at fixed times or last for fixed periods
Governments use fiscal and monetary policies to try and smooth out these extreme ups and downs

question_text: How does 'inflation' cause a reduction in purchasing power?

key_points.text: Inflation means that the general level of prices for goods and services is rising
If prices go up, your fixed amount of money (like a €10 note) can buy fewer goods than before
The purchasing power (what your money can buy) of that money has decreased
For example, if bread costs €1 today and €1.10 next year, your €10 buys less bread next year

question_text: Give an example of a situation where the government uses 'coercion' to improve the economy.

key_points.text: Mandatory taxes (tax collection is forced and legally required)
The money is used to fund public goods like police and defense, which would not be funded privately
Environmental regulations (companies are forced to meet certain pollution limits)
These rules stop companies from creating negative externalities like pollution, making society better off

question_text: What does it mean for a household to be 'financially illiterate'?

key_points.text: It means the household lacks the knowledge and skills to manage their money effectively
They may struggle with understanding concepts like interest rates, savings plans, or risks
This can lead to them making poor financial choices like taking out expensive loans or getting into debt
Financial education is often needed to help them make better intertemporal choices (Domain E)

question_text: Explain the role of supply in determining the market price of a good.

key_points.text: Supply is the amount of the good available to be sold
If supply increases (shifts right, more is available), this creates a surplus at the old price
To sell the extra goods, sellers must lower the price, driving the market price down
If supply decreases (shifts left), this causes a shortage, and the market price will rise

question_text: What is the difference between 'absolute advantage' and 'comparative advantage'?

key_points.text: Absolute Advantage: A country can produce a good using fewer resources than another country (it is simply better/faster at producing)
Comparative Advantage: A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
Trade is always based on comparative advantage for both parties to gain
A country can have an absolute advantage in everything but only a comparative advantage in one thing

question_text: What is 'human capital' and why is it important for economic success?

key_points.text: Human capital is the knowledge, skills, and health that people have and use in their work
It is increased through education, training, and experience
Higher human capital leads to higher productivity (people can make more in the same time)
This makes the country's labor more valuable and leads to higher national income and better standards of living

question_text: Explain the concept of 'net profit' for a business.

key_points.text: Net profit is the final amount of money a business has left over
It is calculated after deducting all costs (fixed and variable) and taxes from the total revenue
Net Profit = Total Revenue - Total Costs - Taxes
This profit can then be reinvested in the business or paid out to the owners/shareholders

question_text: How does a reduction in taxes affect a consumer's decision-making due to scarcity?

key_points.text: Lower taxes mean the consumer's disposable income (the money they can spend) increases
The budget line shifts outwards, meaning they have more resources to satisfy their wants (less scarcity)
This allows them to afford combinations of goods and services they couldn't afford before
They can now choose to consume more or save more (intertemporal exchange)

question_text: What is the 'opportunity cost' of spending money on national defense?

key_points.text: The opportunity cost is the value of the 'next best' public good the government could have bought instead
It could be the new hospitals, schools, or roads that are not built due to the spending on defense
This illustrates the scarcity of government funds (Domain B)
The government must constantly weigh the cost and benefit of one choice against another

question_text: Explain the concept of 'default risk' for a lender (like a bank).

key_points.text: Default risk is the risk that a borrower (a person or company) will not pay back their loan or debt
Banks manage this risk by checking the borrower's credit history and asking for security (collateral)
The higher the risk of default, the higher the interest rate the bank will charge the borrower
This is a key consideration in all exchange over time transactions (Domain E)

question_text: In a market, what is the effect of an increase in the cost of raw materials on the market price?

key_points.text: Higher raw material costs increase the costs of production for the supplier
This means they are willing to supply less at the old price (the supply curve shifts left)
This creates a shortage in the market at the old price
The price mechanism reacts, and the equilibrium market price will rise

question_text: What is the key problem with 'barter' that led to the invention of money?

key_points.text: The need for a double coincidence of wants (Domain C)
This means the person selling goods A must want to buy good B, AND the person selling goods B must want to buy good A
Finding this match is very time-consuming and inefficient (high transaction costs)
Money acts as a medium of exchange, solving this problem and making trade simple

question_text: Why do cartels often fail or break apart (Domain F)?

key_points.text: There is a strong incentive for individual members to 'cheat (the collective action problem)
A cheating member can lower their price slightly to sell more and gain more profit for themselves
Once one member cheats, the others must also lower their price to compete, causing the price to collapse
Cartels are also illegal in most countries (coercion is used to prevent them)

question_text: What is 'liquidity' for a business and why is it important?

key_points.text: Liquidity is a company's ability to meet its short-term financial obligations (pay bills that are due soon)
It means having enough cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash
A liquid company is considered financially healthy and less likely to go bankrupt
One key financial figure to check liquidity is the current ratio (current assets / current liabilities)

question_text: Define 'monopolistic competition' and give an example.

key_points.text: A market with many sellers (like perfect competition)
But the products are differentiated (not identical), e.g., different types of coffee or restaurants
Firms compete on price, quality, and marketing, having a little control over their own prices (price makers)
Entry and exit to the market are relatively easy

question_text: How does the Central Bank's increase of the interest rate affect the economy?

key_points.text: Banks must pay more to borrow from the Central Bank (higher interest rates)
This makes all other loan interest rates (for mortgages, etc.) in the economy go up
This discourages borrowing and investment (Domain E) and encourages saving
This slows down spending and is mainly used to lower high inflation

question_text: What is the concept of 'market transparency'?

key_points.text: It means all participants (buyers and sellers) have full access to all relevant information
This includes knowing all the prices being offered and the quality of the products
Low transparency can lead to asymmetric information and poor decision-making
It is a requirement for a perfectly competitive market to work efficiently (Domain D)

question_text: Give an example of a positive externality.

key_points.text: A neighbor maintains a beautiful garden (consumption activity)
The neighbors around them benefit from the nice view and higher property value without paying for the garden
A company investing in basic scientific research; the knowledge can be used by everyone
The social benefit of the action is higher than the private benefit, leading to underproduction in a free market

question_text: Why do governments sometimes offer subsidies to address positive externalities?

key_points.text: Positive externalities lead to the good or service being underproduced by the market
A subsidy lowers the cost for the producer or consumer (shifting supply right)
This encourages more production or consumption of the beneficial good (e.g., vaccines or solar panels)
The goal is to push the output level toward the socially optimal (best for society) quantity

question_text: In the context of scarcity, what does the phrase 'there is no such thing as a free lunch' mean?

key_points.text: It means that even if something appears to be free to you, it still uses scarce resources to produce it
Those resources could have been used for something else (there is an opportunity cost)
Someone, somewhere, is paying for it (e.g., the government through taxes or the company as a promotion)
Every production decision involves a cost, even if it is not a direct price to the consumer (Domain B)

question_text: What is the function of a Unit of Account for money?

key_points.text: It means money provides a common and accepted way to measure value
All goods and services can be priced in the same unit (e.g., the Euro)
This makes it easy to compare the relative worth of two different goods (e.g., is a house worth 10 cars?)
Without this function, exchange would be very confusing (Domain C)

question_text: What is the dependency ratio in an aging country like the Netherlands?

key_points.text: It is the ratio of the number of people who are not working (young children and retirees)
To the number of people who are working (the labor force)
As the population ages, the number of retirees increases, making the ratio higher
A higher dependency ratio puts more financial strain on the working population (higher taxes/contributions)

question_text: How does a government use public spending to try to end a recession (expansionary fiscal policy)?

key_points.text: The government increases its spending (e.g., on infrastructure projects like roads)
This directly creates demand for goods, services, and labor (new jobs are created)
This stimulates the economy, increasing production and reducing unemployment
The goal is to shift the economy out of the recession phase of the business cycle

question_text: Why do interest rates for short-term loans tend to be lower than for long-term loans?

key_points.text: There is less risk for the bank when lending money for a shorter period
There is less time for the borrower's financial situation to worsen (less default risk)
There is also less risk of the money's value being destroyed by inflation over a long time
Lenders need to be paid a higher premium (interest) to give up their money for a very long time (Domain E)

question_text: What is a production possibility curve (PPC) and what does it illustrate?

key_points.text: It is a graph showing the maximum possible output of two goods or services
It is based on the assumption that all the economy's resources are being used efficiently
It clearly illustrates scarcity (points outside the curve are impossible) (Domain B)
The shape of the curve shows the opportunity cost (the trade-off) of making more of one good instead of the other

question_text: How does the specialization of countries lead to a higher global output (Domain C)?

key_points.text: Each country focuses its resources on the goods where it has a comparative advantage
Resources are used where they are most productive, avoiding costly inefficiencies
Because production costs are lower everywhere, more goods are produced in total around the world
Through exchange (trade), every country can consume more than it could produce alone

question_text: Explain the role of the European Union (EU) in facilitating exchange (Domain C).

key_points.text: The EU created a single market where goods, services, labor, and capital can move freely
It removed trade barriers like tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas between member states
It established a common currency (the Euro) for most members, eliminating exchange rate costs
This makes exchange cheaper, faster, and simpler, boosting trade and specialization

question_text: What is the income elasticity of demand and what does a negative value indicate?

key_points.text: It measures how much the quantity demanded changes when a consumer's income changes
A negative value indicates that the good is an inferior good (Domain D)
This means that as income rises, people buy less of the good (they switch to better alternatives)
A positive value indicates a normal good

question_text: How can a household use a loan (intertemporal exchange) to improve its welfare?

key_points.text: A loan allows the household to consume now instead of having to wait to save up (e.g., buying a house)
They pay for the current consumption with future income, spreading the cost over time
For big purchases like a house, the benefit of having it now usually outweighs the cost of the interest paid
However, they must be sure they can pay back the principal and interest in the future (risk management)

question_text: Explain the concept of diminishing returns to scale in production.

key_points.text: It is a point where adding an extra unit of an input (like one more worker) leads to a smaller increase in total output
For example, adding a 10th worker to a small coffee shop won't increase coffee production as much as adding the 2nd worker
The reason is often overcrowding, too many managers, or running out of fixed resources (like the size of the building)
It affects the marginal cost of production, causing it to eventually rise as output increases

question_text: What is the difference between a deficit and debt for a government?

key_points.text: Deficit is a flow; it's the amount the government spends more than it collects in taxes in one year
Debt is a stock; it's the total accumulated amount of money the government owes from all past deficits (minus surpluses)
A deficit adds to the total debt
Paying the interest on the debt is a significant expense in the government's annual budget (Domain E)

question_text: How can cooperation (Domain F) between a company and a trade union benefit both parties?

key_points.text: Cooperation can lead to a collective labor agreement (CAO) that provides a stable working environment
The company gains by avoiding strikes and conflicts, which hurt production and profit
The workers gain by securing better wages and working conditions than they could get individually
Both parties achieve a better overall outcome than if they constantly tried to work against each other

question_text: What is the main goal of a Trade Union (vakbond) in the labor market?

key_points.text: To improve the wages, job security, and working conditions for its members (workers)
They achieve this by using the collective bargaining power of all members together (cooperation)
They negotiate directly with employers or employer organizations on behalf of all workers
If negotiations fail, they may use collective action like strikes to force an agreement

question_text: Explain what a speculator does in a market.

key_points.text: A speculator is a person who buys an asset (like stocks, property, or currency)
With the goal of making a quick profit from changes in its market price
They believe the asset is currently undervalued and will rise in price in the near future
They play a key role in the stability and liquidity of financial markets (Domain D and E)

question_text: What is the concept of a capital-intensive production process?

key_points.text: A production method that uses a relatively large amount of capital (machines, technology, factories)
And a relatively small amount of labor (human workers)
Examples include automated car production lines or chemical plants
This is often used in rich countries due to the high cost of labor and is a source of high productivity

question_text: What is the concept of a labor-intensive production process?

key_points.text: A production method that uses a relatively large amount of labor (human workers)
And a relatively small amount of capital (machines and technology)
Examples include handmade crafts, certain types of farming, or customer service call centers
This is often used in developing countries where labor is cheaper and more available than capital

question_text: Why is trust important for the function of money (Domain C)?

key_points.text: Money is primarily fiat money (its value is not based on gold, but on belief)
People must trust that the money they accept today will be accepted by others tomorrow
They must also trust that the government/central bank will not let the value be destroyed by extreme inflation
Without trust, money loses its function as a medium of exchange, and people would resort to barter

question_text: How does the Central Bank's reserve requirement affect money creation?

key_points.text: The reserve requirement is the minimum fraction of deposits that commercial banks must keep in reserve (not lend out)
The money a bank lends out is how new money is created in the economy (money multiplier)
If the Central Bank increases the reserve requirement, banks can lend out less money
This slows down the process of money creation (Domain C) and helps control inflation

question_text: Explain the concept of moral hazard in financial markets.

key_points.text: It is a situation where one party (the 'agent') takes increased risks
Because the costs of those risks will be borne by another party (the 'principal')
Example: A person with full insurance might be less careful with their bicycle than a person without insurance
Example: A bank might take excessive risks if it expects the government will bail it out with taxpayer money

question_text: What is a progressive tax system?

key_points.text: A tax system where the tax rate increases as the taxpayer's income increases
People with higher incomes pay a larger percentage of their income in taxes
The goal is to achieve income redistribution (taking from the rich to help the poor)
The Dutch income tax system uses progressive tax brackets

question_text: How does a regressive tax system affect people with different income levels?

key_points.text: A regressive tax system is one where the tax rate decreases as the taxpayer's income increases
This means people with lower incomes pay a larger percentage of their income in tax than the rich
Sales tax (VAT) is often seen as regressive because poor people spend a greater percentage of their income than rich people do
It generally increases income inequality

question_text: In the context of government finance, what is a transfer payment?

key_points.text: Money paid by the government to individuals for which no current good or service is received in return
It is not counted as part of GDP because it is a transfer of money, not payment for production
Examples include unemployment benefits, pensions, and child support payments
Transfer payments are a key tool for income redistribution and social security

question_text: What is the difference between a share (stock) and a bond?

key_points.text: Share (Stock): Represents ownership in a company; the shareholder earns a dividend and profits from rising prices
Bond: Represents a debt (a loan) to a company or government; the bondholder earns fixed interest payments and gets the loan back at the end
Shares are riskier but have higher potential returns; bonds are generally safer
Both are ways for entities to raise capital for investment (Domain E)

question_text: How does the concept of risk aversion influence consumer choices?

key_points.text: Risk aversion means that people prefer a certain outcome over a risky outcome with the same expected value
Risk-averse people are willing to pay a premium (cost) to avoid risk (e.g., buying insurance)
It influences intertemporal choices, often leading to people choosing safer savings accounts over risky stock market investments
It explains why low-risk loans have lower interest rates than high-risk loans (Domain E)

question_text: Define external costs and give an example.

key_points.text: External costs are the negative side effects of production or consumption that are paid for by society or a third party
These costs are not included in the private market price (the producer does not pay for them)
Example: The cost of cleaning up river pollution caused by a factory, which is paid for by taxpayers
They represent a market failure because the price does not reflect the true social cost

question_text: What is the multiplier effect of government spending?

key_points.text: It is the idea that an initial increase in government spending (or investment) causes a larger overall increase in national income (GDP)
When the government spends money, that money becomes income for someone else
That person then spends part of that income, which becomes income for another person, and so on
The total increase in GDP is a multiple of the original government spending amount

question_text: What is the function of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in global exchange?

key_points.text: It is an international organization that deals with the rules of trade between nations
Its main goal is to help trade flow smoothly, predictably, and as freely as possible (Domain C)
It does this by encouraging countries to reduce trade barriers like tariffs and quotas
It also provides a system for resolving trade disputes between member countries

question_text: How does a reduction in the cost of production affect the equilibrium price and quantity?

key_points.text: Lower costs mean firms are willing to supply more at any given price
The supply curve shifts to the right (an increase in supply)
The new equilibrium price will be lower (good for consumers)
The new equilibrium quantity traded in the market will be higher

question_text: What are economies of scale for a business?

key_points.text: It means the average cost of producing one unit of a good decreases
As the business increases the total amount of goods it produces (gets bigger)
This is because large firms can get discounts on bulk buying or use specialized, efficient machinery
It makes it hard for small, new companies to compete with large, established ones

question_text: Why do most real-world economies today operate as mixed economies?

key_points.text: A mixed economy combines elements of a free market (private ownership and price mechanism)
With elements of central planning (government intervention and regulation)
It allows the efficiency of the market to drive growth, while the government corrects market failures (e.g., pollution, monopolies)
Purely free markets or centrally planned economies are prone to instability or inefficiency

question_text: What is the role of the stock market (or bourse) in the economy?

key_points.text: It is a market where shares of ownership (stocks) in publicly traded companies are bought and sold
It allows companies to raise large amounts of capital for investment and growth (Domain E)
It gives individual investors a chance to participate in the profits of successful companies
The price movements reflect investor expectations about the future value of companies

question_text: In the context of scarcity, what does rational choice mean for a consumer?

key_points.text: It means the consumer makes decisions that maximize their utility (satisfaction or happiness)
They choose the combination of goods that gives them the greatest satisfaction within their limited budget
A rational consumer weighs the marginal benefit of consuming one more item against its marginal cost (price)
It assumes people are generally self-interested and make choices based on available information

question_text: What is the definition of a substitute good and how does it affect demand?

key_points.text: A substitute good is a product that can be used in place of another product (e.g., butter and margarine)
If the price of good A rises, the demand for its substitute, good B, will increase (shift right)
The availability of good substitutes makes the demand for a product more elastic (sensitive to price changes)
Consumers switch easily to the cheaper option (Domain D)

question_text: What is the definition of a complementary good and how does it affect demand?

key_points.text: A complementary good is a product that is consumed along with another product (e.g., cars and gasoline, coffee and sugar)
If the price of good A rises, the demand for its complement, good B, will decrease (shift left)
People buy fewer cars if the price of gasoline goes up a lot
The demand for the two goods moves in the same direction

question_text: Explain what a speculative bubble is in a financial market.

key_points.text: It is a situation where the price of an asset (like housing or stocks) rises rapidly and excessively
The price rise is not justified by the asset's true, fundamental value or future profitability
The price increases simply because people expect others to buy it later for an even higher price
Bubbles always burst eventually, causing the price to crash and often leading to financial crises

question_text: What is the role of insurance in managing risk (Domain E)?

key_points.text: Insurance allows individuals to transfer the financial risk of a major loss (like fire or theft) to a company
The insurance company pools the small payments (premiums) from many people
This allows the individual to avoid the single, large, uncertain cost of the loss
It converts a large, unknown risk into a small, known cost (the premium)

question_text: What is the difference between short-term and long-term unemployment?

key_points.text: Short-term: People who are out of work for a relatively brief period (e.g., less than six months)
Long-term: People who are continuously out of work for a very long period (e.g., a year or more)
Long-term unemployment is a bigger problem; workers' skills can become outdated (lose human capital)
Long-term unemployed people are often harder to get back into the labor force

question_text: Explain structural unemployment.

key_points.text: Unemployment that occurs because there is a mismatch between the skills workers have and the skills employers need
It can be caused by long-term changes in the economy, like the rise of automation or new technology
Example: Coal miners losing their jobs when the country switches to renewable energy
The solution requires workers to get retraining (new human capital) to fill the new job vacancies

question_text: What is frictional unemployment?

key_points.text: Unemployment that occurs when people are voluntarily changing jobs or entering the labor force for the first time
It is a natural and temporary part of a healthy, dynamic economy
Example: A student who just graduated and is actively looking for their first job
It is usually short-term, as the person expects to find a suitable job soon

question_text: How does technological unemployment occur?

key_points.text: It is a form of structural unemployment where people lose their jobs because their tasks are taken over by machines or software (automation)
Technology increases productivity by doing the work faster and cheaper than humans
Example: A factory worker replaced by a robot, or a cashier replaced by a self-checkout machine
While some jobs are lost, new jobs are often created in developing and maintaining the new technology

question_text: Explain the relationship between scarcity and the need for a pricing system (Domain D).

key_points.text: Scarcity means there is less of a good than people want at a price of zero
If things were not scarce, they would be free, and there would be no need to decide who gets what
Because of scarcity, a price is needed to ration (distribute) the limited supply
The market price ensures that only those who are willing and able to pay can get the good

question_text: What is economic inequality?

key_points.text: It is the unequal distribution of income and/or wealth among people in a society
It is often measured using tools like the Gini coefficient
High inequality means a small percentage of people own a large majority of the wealth
Governments try to reduce extreme inequality through progressive taxes and transfer payments

question_text: How does the value of money change during a period of deflation?

key_points.text: Deflation is when the general level of prices is falling (negative inflation)
The purchasing power of money is increasing
The same amount of money can buy more goods and services than before
However, deflation can cause problems because people delay purchases, hoping prices will fall further

question_text: What is the economic concept of utility?

key_points.text: Utility is the satisfaction, pleasure, or happiness a person gets from consuming a good or service
It is subjective (different for every person)
Rational consumers try to maximize their total utility given their limited resources (scarcity)
Economists assume consumers make choices to achieve the highest possible utility

question_text: Explain the law of diminishing marginal utility.

key_points.text: It states that as a person consumes more and more units of a specific good
The extra satisfaction (marginal utility) they get from each additional unit starts to decrease
Example: The first slice of pizza gives you much more satisfaction than the fifth slice
This explains why consumers are only willing to buy more of a product if the price is lowered

question_text: What is a public-private partnership (PPP) and how does it relate to cooperation (Domain F)?

key_points.text: A PPP is a long-term cooperation agreement between a government entity (public) and a private company
They cooperate to build, finance, and operate public projects (e.g., roads, schools, or IT systems)
The private sector brings efficiency and capital, while the public sector brings funding and manages public interests
It allows the government to deliver large projects it might not have the money or expertise to do alone

question_text: How can a government use regulations to try to prevent monopolies?

key_points.text: Governments use competition laws to monitor the behavior of large companies
They can stop large companies from merging if the merger would create too much market power (less competition)
They can force a monopoly to break up into smaller, competing companies (rarely done)
They can regulate the price a natural monopoly is allowed to charge (price ceiling)

question_text: What is the financial sector and what is its main purpose?

key_points.text: It is the part of the economy made up of banks, insurance companies, stock exchanges, and other financial services
Its main purpose is to facilitate the flow of money between savers/lenders and borrowers/investors (Domain E)
It provides the infrastructure for all economic exchange (payments, loans, and risk management)
It helps the economy grow by efficiently allocating capital to the most productive investments

question_text: What is balance of trade and what is the difference between a surplus and a deficit?

key_points.text: Balance of trade is the difference between a country's total value of exports and its total value of imports
Trade Surplus: The country exports (sells) more goods and services than it imports (buys)
Trade Deficit: The country imports (buys) more goods and services than it exports (sells)
The Netherlands usually has a trade surplus, meaning it earns more from trade than it spends

question_text: How can a government try to reduce a large trade deficit?

key_points.text: Encourage more exports (e.g., by subsidizing exporting companies)
Discourage imports (e.g., by raising taxes on imported goods, known as tariffs)
Encourage domestic consumers to 'buy local' instead of buying imported goods
These policies are often controversial as they reduce the benefits of international exchange

question_text: What is the role of the interest rate in determining exchange rates?

key_points.text: Higher interest rates in a country make savings and investments (like bonds) in that country more attractive to foreign investors
Foreign investors will want to buy that country's currency (e.g., the Euro) to invest
The increased demand for the currency causes its value (the exchange rate) to rise
Lower interest rates lead to capital outflows and a fall in the exchange rate

question_text: Explain the concept of price leadership in an oligopoly (Domain D).

key_points.text: It is a form of implicit cooperation or silent agreement between firms in an oligopoly
One dominant firm (the 'leader') is the first to announce a price change (up or down)
The other firms (the 'followers') then quickly match the price change
This avoids aggressive price wars that hurt everyone and allows the firms to maintain high profits

question_text: What is consumer surplus in a market?

key_points.text: It is the difference between the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good
And the actual price they end up paying in the market
It represents the extra benefit or satisfaction consumers get from a transaction
If the market price falls, consumer surplus increases (the area above the price, below the demand curve)

question_text: What is producer surplus in a market?

key_points.text: It is the difference between the actual price a producer receives for a good
And the minimum price they would have been willing to accept (their marginal cost)
It represents the extra benefit or profit producers get from a transaction
If the market price rises, producer surplus increases (the area below the price, above the supply curve)

question_text: What is the main purpose of the World Bank?

key_points.text: It is an international financial institution that provides loans and grants to the governments of developing countries
Its goal is to reduce poverty and promote shared prosperity
The loans are often for large projects like building infrastructure, improving education, or fighting disease
It facilitates intertemporal exchange and investment on a global scale (Domain E)

question_text: Explain the concept of absolute poverty.

key_points.text: A condition where people are unable to meet their basic needs for survival
Basic needs include sufficient food, clean water, shelter, and essential healthcare
It is often defined by a fixed poverty line (e.g., living on less than $2.15 a day)
It is the most severe form of scarcity and is a major focus for international aid organizations

question_text: Explain the concept of relative poverty.

key_points.text: A condition where people's income is significantly lower than the average income in their country
They can afford basic necessities but cannot participate in activities considered normal for their society
Example: Being unable to afford heating, new clothes, or a school trip that most other people can afford
It is a measure of economic inequality within a wealthy country

question_text: What is the economic concept of a tax base?

key_points.text: The tax base is the total value of the activity, asset, or income that is subject to taxation
For income tax, the tax base is the total income earned by people and companies
For sales tax (VAT), the tax base is the total value of all goods and services sold
The government calculates tax revenue by multiplying the tax rate by the tax base

question_text: How does the price mechanism help solve the basic economic question 'For whom to produce?' (Domain D).

key_points.text: The goods are generally distributed to the people who are willing and able to pay the market price
People with higher incomes (who can afford more) influence what is produced
High demand from people who can pay leads to high prices and signals producers to make more for them
This leads to an efficient, but not necessarily equal, distribution of the goods

question_text: Explain the concept of capital flight.

key_points.text: It is the large and sudden movement of money and assets out of a country
It is usually done by domestic citizens or businesses (not foreign investors)
